title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 55–56
description: Industry structures, ownership, employment practices, industrial crime and technological developments, devices and precise technical word families.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal vocabulary study. The learning targets follow the source pages and relevant exercises; Portuguese translations, English notes and sample sentences are independently authored. No textbook passages, extended exercises or illustrations are reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 55 and Unit 56 teaching pages, contrast tables, technology examples, usage notes, exercises 55.1–55.3 and 56.1–56.4, and matching answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Conservative broad British IPA for short words only where the transcription is sufficiently reliable. IPA is omitted for unverified or longer multiword terms; full connected-speech pronunciations and regional variants are not modelled.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing content and metadata are in English except for Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared source teaching pages, diagrams, tables, notes, exercises and answer key; checked lexical distinctions, register, source provenance and original examples. Performed static validation of JSON structure, required fields, IDs and TTS target handling. No application-level browser or speech tests were conducted.
audit.limitations: No MP3s are bundled. The real VocabLab importer, browser TTS and recognition remain untested. Industry policies, labour-law terminology and technology product examples are used for language study and may vary by country or change over time.

units.title: Unit 55 — Industries: from manufacturing to service
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 55. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish heavy and light industry, manufacturing and services, high-tech and low-tech, and conventional and cutting-edge technologies.
Discuss forms of ownership, subsidies and inward investment in precise economic language.
Describe employment arrangements, industrial production, relocation and workforce retraining using natural collocations.
Recognise exercise-based terminology for exploitative production and unlawful commercial practices.

sectionsChecked: A and B teaching sections, both contrast tables and all word definitions
Exercises 55.1–55.3, including the exercise-only industrial crime terms

items.example: The region has struggled to diversify beyond heavy industry and mining.
items.note: Manufactures large industrial products, such as steel or ships; contrasts with light industry.

items.example: Local officials hope that light industry will create less polluting employment.
items.note: Manufacturing relatively small or less heavy goods; contrasted with heavy industry.

items.example: The manufacturing industry relies on a reliable supply of specialised components.
items.note: Produces physical goods, rather than selling services.

items.example: Employment in the service industry has expanded as tourism has grown.
items.note: Provides services, for example banking or tourism; contrasted with manufacturing.

items.example: A thriving high-technology industry has developed around the research park.
items.note: Industry using sophisticated modern technology; often shortened to high-tech industry.

items.example: Some low-technology industries remain heavily dependent on manual labour.
items.note: Contrasts with high-technology industry; does not necessarily imply poor quality.

items.example: The prototype incorporates cutting-edge technology that has yet to reach mass production.
items.note: Emphasises innovation and the newest advances, unlike established conventional technology.

items.example: The hospital retained conventional technology until the experimental equipment had been evaluated.
items.note: Established and standard methods rather than the newest innovations.

items.example: The proposed privatisation of the railway prompted a parliamentary debate.
items.note: Transfer of ownership or control from the public to the private sector; British spelling.

items.example: The party promised nationalisation of the struggling utility company.
items.note: Transfer of businesses or industries into state ownership; opposite direction from privatisation.

items.example: Supporters of state ownership argued that water supplies should remain publicly controlled.
items.note: Ownership by government; distinct from a partnership shared with private investors.

items.example: The council negotiated a public-private partnership to modernise the city's transport network.
items.note: A collaborative arrangement involving public authorities and private-sector organisations; arrangements vary.

items.example: The government withdrew the subsidy after the factory became profitable.
items.note: Money provided to support an activity or industry; not necessarily a loan.

items.pt: investimento estrangeiro que entra no país
items.example: Tax incentives were introduced to attract inward investment into the region.
items.note: Investment coming into a country, frequently from companies based abroad.

items.pt: trabalho remunerado por produção; pagamento por peça
items.example: Under a piecework arrangement, workers were paid for each completed garment.
items.note: Payment depends on the number of items or tasks completed, rather than simply hours worked.

items.pt: contrato de trabalho sem garantia de horas mínimas
items.example: Employees on zero-hours contracts may find their monthly income unpredictable.
items.note: An employment arrangement without a guaranteed minimum number of paid hours; British usage.

items.pt: estabilidade no emprego; segurança de manutenção do emprego
items.example: The workforce demanded greater job security during the restructuring talks.
items.note: The likelihood of keeping one's job, not protection from physical hazards.

items.example: The audit uncovered child labour in a subcontractor's production chain.
items.note: Employment of children in work inappropriate for their age or harmful to their development.

items.example: Workers sought trade union representation before negotiating new conditions.
items.note: Being represented by an organisation that defends workers' employment interests.

items.example: The trade union called for negotiations over pay and workplace safety.
items.note: British term for a workers' organisation; often simply union.

items.pt: fábrica exploratória com condições precárias de trabalho
items.example: The investigation exposed a sweatshop paying far below the legal minimum wage.
items.note: Disapproving term for a workplace with exploitative conditions and very low pay.

items.pt: recapacitação profissional; formação para uma nova função
items.example: The company funded retraining for employees whose roles had been automated.
items.note: Training again, often to prepare for a different kind of job.

items.example: Reskilling programmes helped technicians move into renewable-energy jobs.
items.note: Developing new skills, especially to adapt to changes in employment demands.

items.example: A multinational acquired the local supplier but kept its engineering team.
items.note: A company operating in several countries; also an adjective as in multinational company.

items.example: Management described the office closures as a cost-cutting exercise.
items.note: A planned attempt to reduce spending; may be a neutral or critical description.

items.pt: transferir-se; mudar de local de operação
items.example: The manufacturer decided to relocate its assembly plant closer to its suppliers.
items.note: Move a business, office or operation to another location; may be transitive or intransitive.

items.pt: transferir a produção para outro local ou produto
items.example: The group intends to switch production to a plant with more efficient equipment.
items.note: Move manufacturing to a different location or change what is being made; context identifies the intended sense.

items.example: A shortage of electronic components delayed assembly of the control boards.
items.note: A part used to make a larger product, system or machine.

items.example: Workers assemble the final units from parts supplied by several factories.
items.note: Put components together; differs from manufacture, which covers the wider process of making goods.

items.example: The company manufactures precision sensors for industrial applications.
items.note: Make goods, usually on an industrial scale; contrasted with merely assembling imported parts.

items.pt: economia baseada em produção exploratória e mão de obra barata
items.section: C · Industrial risks and unlawful practices
items.example: Critics warned that the export strategy could create a sweatshop economy.
items.note: A critical description of an economy dependent on exploitative low-paid production; exercise target.

items.pt: pirataria industrial; falsificação comercial de produtos
items.section: C · Industrial risks and unlawful practices
items.example: The brand reported industrial piracy after counterfeit products appeared on the market.
items.note: In this exercise, illegal copying of branded manufactured goods; distinct from maritime piracy.

items.section: C · Industrial risks and unlawful practices
items.example: The engineer was accused of industrial espionage after confidential designs were leaked.
items.note: Secretly obtaining a competitor's commercially valuable information.

items.section: C · Industrial risks and unlawful practices
items.example: Reproducing the technical manual without permission could constitute copyright infringement.
items.note: Using copyrighted material in a way that violates the right holder's legal rights.

items.section: C · Industrial risks and unlawful practices
items.example: Investigators traced an international money-laundering scheme through several shell companies.
items.note: Disguising the origins of funds obtained through crime.

items.section: C · Industrial risks and unlawful practices
items.example: A black market emerged when imports were restricted.
items.note: Trade outside legal or authorised channels; black market is usually preceded by the.

units.title: Unit 56 — Technology and its impact
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 56. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Technology · devices, systems and specialist terminology
learningObjectives: Identify digital, satellite, wireless, biotechnology and artificial-intelligence terminology accurately.
Use natural names for computing devices and associated functions, including words provided in the exercises.
Distinguish technical, technological, technically, technologically, technician and technique.
Describe devices and interface elements clearly while recognising register and sense differences.

sectionsChecked: Sections A and B, technology/application table, device examples and Language help
Exercises 56.1–56.4, including additional terms and word-family patterns

items.example: Digital technology has transformed the way laboratories record experimental measurements.
items.note: Technology that represents or processes information digitally; contrasted with analogue technology.

items.example: The team chose digital recording to preserve the interview audio without analogue tape.
items.note: Recording sound, images or data as digital information.

items.example: The engineer compared the analogue signal with its digitally sampled counterpart.
items.note: British spelling; US English analog is common in technical contexts.

items.example: The conference centre provides Wi-Fi throughout the building.
items.note: Wireless local networking used to connect devices to a network; not identical to mobile data.

items.example: Satellite communications kept the research vessel in contact with the mainland.
items.note: Sending signals via satellites, particularly over long distances.

items.example: Satellite navigation helped the survey team find the remote site.
items.note: Determining location and routes using satellite positioning systems.

items.example: The driver checked the satnav before leaving the motorway.
items.note: British clipping of satellite navigation, commonly meaning an in-car navigation device or system.

items.example: The ship's global positioning system provided coordinates during the voyage.
items.note: The expanded name of GPS, a satellite-based positioning system.

items.example: The tracker uses GPS to record the vehicle's location.
items.note: Pronounced letter by letter; a positioning system, not a synonym for every satellite navigation service.

items.example: Biotechnology has enabled researchers to develop new diagnostic methods.
items.note: Application of biological processes or organisms in technology and production.

items.example: The course examined how genetic modification can alter crop characteristics.
items.note: Intentional change to genetic material; used as a technology example, not as an endorsement.

items.example: The trial compared disease-resistant crops with conventional varieties.
items.note: Resistant to particular diseases, rather than wholly immune to every disease.

items.example: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to classify large datasets.
items.note: Computational systems performing tasks associated with aspects of human intelligence; often AI.

items.example: The company uses AI to detect anomalies in its manufacturing data.
items.note: The abbreviation of artificial intelligence; spoken as two letters.

items.example: Ergonomics influenced the arrangement of controls on the operator's desk.
items.note: Study of how tasks, tools and environments fit human capabilities and comfort.

items.example: The controller was ergonomically designed to reduce strain during long shifts.
items.note: Designed with attention to comfort, efficiency and human use; not proof of a medical benefit.

items.pt: Bluetooth; tecnologia de conexão sem fio de curto alcance
items.example: The headset connects to the laptop through Bluetooth.
items.note: Wireless technology used for short-range device communication; not a general term for Wi-Fi.

items.pt: entusiasta de tecnologia; pessoa ligada em tecnologia
items.example: As a keen techie, Marta enjoys trying out new interfaces and gadgets.
items.note: Informal and often neutral or affectionate for someone enthusiastic about technology.

items.example: Her smartphone doubles as a camera and a navigation device.
items.note: A mobile phone with substantial computing and internet functions.

items.pt: fone de ouvido para uso sem as mãos
items.example: He used a hands-free earpiece while dictating notes.
items.note: An earpiece that permits communication without holding the phone.

items.example: Staff use a smart ID card to enter the secure laboratory.
items.note: An identification card with electronically stored information or authentication features.

items.example: The technician brought a laptop to configure the motor controller.
items.note: A portable computer; notebook is also used for this sense.

items.example: She prefers a lightweight notebook when travelling to conferences.
items.note: Here an alternative term for a laptop, not a paper notebook.

items.example: The data-acquisition software runs on a dedicated desktop computer.
items.note: A computer normally used in one place, unlike a laptop.

items.example: The old MP3 player still works despite its worn battery.
items.note: A portable device designed to play compressed digital audio files.

items.example: The games console can also stream films and music.
items.note: British form of game console; specialised hardware for video games.

items.pt: tablet; computador em formato de prancheta
items.example: The field researcher entered observations directly on a tablet.
items.note: Portable touchscreen computer; not the same sense as a medicinal tablet.

items.example: The touchscreen allows operators to change settings without a mouse.
items.note: Screen that registers touch input; can also be used attributively.

items.example: An e-reader is convenient for carrying several technical books on a journey.
items.note: A device primarily for reading electronic books; different from a general-purpose tablet.

items.example: The interactive flat-screen TV let viewers select additional programme information.
items.note: A flat-screen television supporting user interaction, beyond passive viewing.

items.example: Restarting the router restored the office network connection.
items.note: Device directing network traffic among devices or between networks.

items.example: The report contains a technical explanation of the measurement procedure.
items.note: Relates to specialist methods, knowledge or equipment; not identical to technological.

items.example: The company faces technological challenges as its products become more complex.
items.note: Concerns technology and its development or application, rather than technical expertise alone.

items.pt: tecnicamente; do ponto de vista técnico
items.example: The modification is technically feasible, although it would be expensive.
items.note: Here means from the standpoint of technical capabilities or requirements.

items.example: The newer system is technologically more advanced than its predecessor.
items.note: Adverb concerning technology or technological advancement, not strict factual definitions.

items.example: A laboratory technician calibrated the instruments before the trial.
items.note: Person trained to carry out practical technical work.

items.example: The study introduced a new technique for reducing electrical noise.
items.note: A method or skill used to achieve something; distinguish from technology in general.

items.example: Click the thumbnail to open the photograph at full resolution.
items.note: A small preview of a larger image; exercise-only computer vocabulary.

items.pt: nerd de computação; pessoa obcecada por computadores
items.example: He jokingly calls himself a computer nerd because he spends weekends coding.
items.note: May be teasing or disparaging; contrasted in the book with the less negative techie.

items.example: The university launched an app for checking laboratory reservations.
items.note: Informal shortening of application, meaning a software program.

items.example: An abstract animation appeared when the screensaver activated.
items.note: On-screen image or animation shown after inactivity; not necessarily used for modern display protection.

items.pt: espaço físico ocupado; área de instalação
items.example: The redesigned printer has a smaller footprint, leaving more room on the desk.
items.note: Here means the physical space equipment occupies, not a carbon or digital footprint.

items.example: Select the settings icon to open the configuration menu.
items.note: Small visual symbol representing a function, application or file.

items.pt: touchpad; superfície de toque do notebook
items.example: The presenter used the laptop's trackpad instead of a separate mouse.
items.note: Touch-sensitive pointing device commonly built into laptops.

items.pt: tecnologia; conjunto de técnicas e recursos tecnológicos
items.example: Advances in technology have reshaped industrial control systems.
items.note: The general field of technological methods and tools; distinct from an individual technique.

items.example: Technically, the proposal meets the requirements, but several practical concerns remain.
items.note: Here technically means according to a strict interpretation of the facts, not in an engineering sense.
